title: Suunto Run 2 In-Depth Review: Worth The Premium?
content:
I’ve now been wearing the Suunto Run 2 for exactly one month straight, 24×7, for every workout from run to swim to ride to strength, and everything else in between. The Suunto Run 2 takes the existing Suunto Run 1 and elevates it a fair bit with offline mapping, a new brighter display, and a much improved optical heart rate sensor. They also increased GPS battery claims by about 30%, though smartwatch battery claims went down slightly.

Suunto seemed laser-focused on improving the things people rightfully complained about in the Run 1 and addressing those in the Run 2. Albeit, it now costs $100 more (and nobody complained about the price being too low last time). I suppose you can’t win them all.

The thing to understand about the Suunto Run series is that it’s hardly focused on just runners. In the same way that Garmin’s Forerunner series is hardly for just runners. Both these watches can just as easily be used for triathletes and any other sports that you can throw at it. And I’ve done just that.

With that, let’s get right into it.

What’s New:

The Suunto Run 2 takes the existing Suunto Run 1 from last year and turns it into something that’s more akin to a Suunto Race 2S. Except it’s still called the Suunto Run series, despite being just as capable a multisport watch as a running watch. While last year Suunto pitched the first Suunto Run as an inexpensive running watch, this second-generation model shouldn’t be viewed through that restricted lens.

Here’s what’s changed since the Suunto Run 1:

– Increased display brightness up to 2,000 nits (previous panel was ~1,000 nits)
– Same 1.32” display size as before
– Updated GPS chipset, though still multi-band/dual-frequency
– Notably new optical HR sensor that’s substantially better than before
– Increased GPS battery claims from 20hrs to 30hrs+ (depending on modes)
– Decreased daily smartwatch usage claim from 12 days to 10 days.
– Added offline map capability (download maps)
– Added EnergySense feature for run pacing
– Added HeatStrain Score
– Roughly the same weight as before (35g vs 36g on previous unit)
– Base price increased from $249 to $349USD (or from 249EUR to 349EUR
– Now offered in either 4GB or 64GB models ($349/$399)

In any case, keeping in mind the Suunto Run series still operates on a different operating system than the rest of Suunto’s watches, there remain some restrictions there (such as not supporting any apps in the Suunto App Store, and not supporting structured workouts from 3rd-party platforms). Further, it has fewer sport modes (~35) than the 95+ sport modes on the rest of the Suunto watches. But otherwise, it’s largely the same, minus a few little software quirks here and there that I discuss below.

The unit comes in three color options: Black, green, or white.

In The Box:

The design of the Suunto Run 2 box isn’t much different than other Suunto boxes from the last few years, but I’ve gotta say – every time I open one of the Suunto boxes, it’s one of the cleanest and best-done variants in the industry today. Of course, they took inspiration from Apple Watch boxes years ago, but the little touches on design/photography are well done.

In any case, once you extract all the pieces, here’s what you’ve got:

It’s really pretty straightforward:

– The watch pod
– The band/strap
– The charging cable
– A book you won’t read
– Some other pamphlets you also probably won’t read
– A few stickers you might use

And here’s a closer look at things:

As always, the unboxing section isn’t complicated, so let’s get right into using the watch.

The Basics:

For this first bit, I’m going to dive into all the basic features of the watch, things like activity tracking, daily usage, sleep tracking, and so on. Plus some bits from the Suunto App in those categories. In the next section I’ll cover all the sport-related aspects (including navigation).

The Suunto Run 2 mirrors the also-recent Suunto Race 3S in terms of the Suunto 3-button layout. This means there are two main buttons on the right side, plus a Digital Crown (that also acts as a button). The upper right button goes straight to accessing the most recent sport profile, the middle accesses your ‘Today’s Plan’ and the rest of the sport modes, and the bottom button acts as an escape. The Digital Crown also allows you to access the widgets. On top of that, you’ve got the touchscreen display.

If you’re familiar with other Suunto watches, the Suunto Run 2 might cause you to stumble a little bit with the user interface. While it is similar to other Suunto watches, the Suunto Run 1 & Run 2 run a slightly different operating system than all other Suunto watches. The differences are minor, but enough that muscle-memory tasks (like tapping the upper-right button to select a different sport mode) will cause some stumbles until you re-map that to the middle button instead. It’s no biggie if coming from any other brand watch, and after nearly a month of wearing it, I’ve mostly gotten used to it.

In any case, as for the display, the Suunto Run 2 uses a 2,000-nit display. It’s been perfectly fine in all my outside testing here in the Mediterranean over the last month, even on the sunniest of days. That said, as I noted in my Suunto Race 3S review, launching with a 2,000-nit display in 2026 at this price point is a bit dicey. Companies like Amazfit are putting in 3,000-nit displays in the Balance 3 at the same price point. Again, the display is perfectly fine, but if Suunto is pitching this as a premium budget watch (as weird as that sounds), then it should contain premium parts.

In any case, scrolling down from the watch face, you’ve got the widgets, which include things like steps, training volume/metrics, the weather, and more. It’s funny to see again the differences here from the other Suunto watches, for things like a lack of a specific HRV widget for example (which is on the Suunto Race 3S and other watches), and instead rolling that into the “Recovery” widget.

Nonetheless, all the things are still there, just the deck chairs in slightly different places. And as you’d expect, you can tap into any of these items to see an expanded view of them, such as steps, weather, sleep, etc.

In terms of things like sleep tracking, I haven’t had any accuracy issues here. It’s been basically spot-on with all my other wearables in this realm, and of course, the actual times I went to sleep and woke up. Note that I don’t compare sleep phases/stages, because doing so is peak faux-science. The best-case reference devices you can use to do so are only about 80% accurate, which isn’t all that great (and again, that’s a best-case scenario in perfect lab conditions). Thus, we’d never compare a heart rate sensor to a chest strap that was wrong 20% of the time. Therefore, I’m not gonna do it here either.

Of course, all of this data is mostly driven by looking at your heart rate and other movement sensor data. The Run 2 features a new heart rate sensor on the back (same as the also-new Suunto Race 3S). This sensor is a big step up from the previous Suunto sensors, which didn’t have a history of being super awesome.

In terms of a few other odds and ends, the unit is sold in two variants in terms of storage. One option is at 4GB, and the other at 64GB. This allows for more maps, but most notably also offline music that you’re never going to put on the unit. Sure, it can technically support putting MP3 files via USB cable. But there’s no support for streaming services (e.g., Spotify/etc), because those walled gardens went up years ago, and Suunto was left out in the cold (and that’s not gonna change anytime soon). Still, the option technically exists to stick MP3 files and use Bluetooth headphones to play back the music.

For everyone else, you’ll just use the Media Controls option, which controls music/podcasts/etc on your phone from the watch. Though, I often find that quite finicky. As of this very moment, I’m playing music on my phone, and the watch doesn’t show anything in Media Controls.

Sigh. But when it does, here’s what it looks like (in this case, a few seconds later it decided to enumerate for its photo shoot):

As for smartphone notifications, that too can be finicky as to whether or not they show up. But when they do, here’s what they look like:

Note that there is no flashlight built into this watch. I’m not sure if Suunto got spooked with their current lawsuit fiasco (TLDR: They picked a fight with Garmin, and Garmin fought back against Suunto’s Vertical 2 flashlight). Either way, there isn’t a physical LED flashlight here, but there is a display-based one. I’ve used it a few times for some random under-the-bed type tasks, and it’s OK enough, but it’s no real flashlight either.

When it comes to daily battery life, I’ve been using the always-on mode this entire time. And with roughly 1-3 hours of GPS time per day, I’m getting roughly 4-5 days of battery life between charges. I’m OK with that, though, as I’ll cover in the GPS battery section, that battery life seems to be falling notably short of expectations.

In terms of charging, it uses the same charger as the rest of the recent Suunto watches, which is a magnetic charger that works perfectly fine. It even has a nice braided cable, something that Garmin only offers on their $3,000+ MARQ watches.

Finally, I do want to mention briefly that I’m not in love with the strap/band. Specifically, the tiny little doohickey at the end that keeps the band from flapping around. This doohickey portion that goes through the band is simply not big enough, perhaps 1mm too small (maybe 0.5mm too small), and thus it’s constantly popping off.

I know this sounds trivial, and sure I could go buy another band, but equally, it’s just as if nobody actually wore this thing.

In fact, one day while out gravel riding, I paused for a second to grab some stuff out of my hydration pack, and when I did so, it caught the strap of my watch and actually removed the whole thing and flung it out into the bushes (because it undoes so easily). Not a huge deal, as I was able to go find it, but frankly, I’ve never had that happen in my life before. Let alone the strap unhinging on a multiple-times-a-day basis.

Ok, with that, let’s get into the sports bits.

Sports & Navigation:

The Suunto Run 2 is definitely not just a watch for runners. It’s a true and fully capable multisport watch that can be used for running, cycling, swimming, and a gazillion other sports (including triathlon). And in fact, I pretty evenly spread my time out among those sports and more during my testing.

To start a workout, you’ll tap the middle left button. This then shows anything in our ‘Today’s Plan’ section, which can be structured workouts you’ve saved. Below that are your sport modes:

The Suunto Run 2 has 35 sport profiles on it, which are as follows:

Running, Indoor Cycling, Cycling, Trail Running, Pool Swimming, Openwater Swimming, Track Running, marathon, Treadmill, Vertical Running, Walking, Hiking, Trekking, Mountaineering, Climbing, Triathlon, Orienteering, Cross Training, Mountain Biking, Jump Rope, Indoor Rowing, Crosstrainer, Aerobics, Weight Training, Circuit Training, Stretching, Boxing, Yoga/Pilates, Cross-country Skiing, Alpine Skiing, Snowboarding, Tennis, Badminton, Outdoor Training, Indoor Training

Once you choose a given sport profile, you can then select to enable different features for it, such as following a structured workout, navigating a route/point of interest/bearing, as well as enabling certain targets, like a distance/calorie/pace/duration target.

It’ll also show you how much battery is remaining for that particular battery mode/configuration. Meaning if you get ready to start a workout and you realize you only have 2 hours of battery remaining, but need 4 hours, you can change to other battery modes, including performance, endurance, and power saving. These toggle various features on/off to eke out a bit more battery. I’ve generally found that the Suunto Run 2 overestimates how much battery it has. More on that in a second.

Anyway, in my case, I’ll pick a course for today: This straightforward trail run I did the other day that goes up a mountain and comes back down again:

I do wish I could see more details about the route before (or even after) I select it, such as rendering the actual map below it, rendering the elevation profile, etc. I create routes all the time for trail runs, and while I usually just know it’s the most recent one, it’d be handy to see exactly where this is – rather than just on an empty black screen.

In any case, we’ll head out and start running. You’ll see your normal data on the screen as you’ve configured in the settings.

You’ll also see your navigation and map fields as well. In my case you can see the upcoming route shown on the map, as well as distance remaining.

Then, you’ll also see an elevation profile of the route and where you stand in that situation:

If you go off-route, you’ll get a buzz that you’re off-route, and you can check the map page to see how you managed to screw up. There’s no automatic re-routing; you’ll just want to get yourself back to the course/route itself.

There’s also the new Energy Sense feature, which tells you how much juice it thinks you have left in the tank at that given intensity level, in distance. Suunto bills it to be used in a race-like situation, though there’s no need to do that. You could use it in everyday training as well.

In many ways, it’s got similarities to Garmin’s Stamina feature that’s been around for a number of years (and recently expanded to include both pace and heart rate stamina zones). Now, to be clear, I don’t really ever consult Garmin’s Stamina feature, as I don’t find it super useful.

That said, once you start using a Suunto and a Garmin side-by-side, you quickly realize the fatal flaw in Suunto’s implementation: It has nothing to do with energy (per the name EnergySense), but instead, Pace. It should be renamed “PaceSense”. That’s because the Suunto watch only looks at your pace, not your heart rate.

The easiest way to see this is to simply go down a hill (like above, showing a reduced 55%, when seconds before it was in the 90s). This isn’t because my heart rate is high (it’s not, it’s just 152bpm). But instead, because I’m going faster down a hill (4:06/km, or about 6:50/mi). Yet, when I’m going up a hill at a harder intensity like below (161bpm at 5:18/km or 8:32/mi), now I have somehow more Endurance (88%).

Again, I don’t really understand the point of calling this EnergySense, when it doesn’t look at energy at all (e.g., heart rate, or even calories). Instead, it’s purely looking at pacing, and even if you have a perfectly flat course, when looking at a longer event, like a marathon, how you pace energy-wise is just as much a function of heart rate as it is of pace. And further, to that extent, your ‘Endurance’ isn’t going to be a result of your pace, but of how hard your body is working to maintain that pace. I’m honestly baffled that this is as shortsighted as it is, even being marketed as a beta feature. Did nobody run with this anywhere with hills?

In any case, speaking of the data fields you’ve set up, these are configurable in the Suunto App, and you can customize them on a per-sport profile basis. I still wish I could just tweak existing core sport profiles, rather than having to create duplicates – but that’s just the way Suunto’s been for years.

Oh, speaking of things in the app, this is where you can download maps to the Suunto Run 2. As noted earlier, there is a 4GB and a 64GB model. The thing is, Suunto’s maps are divided up into very small regions, so you can pretty easily get away with just the 4GB model. Especially if you don’t do a ton of traveling. Realistically, I think Suunto could have just gotten away with a single 8GB or 16GB model and called it done. For example, while all of France would be 7GB, the region around Paris would only be 200MB (0.2GB).

In any event, once your workout is completed, you’ll see the details on the watch or in the Suunto App. For example, here on the Suunto App:

Beyond singular workouts, Suunto is also tracking your overall training load and recovery stats. Starting with training load, it’ll track that a few different ways, the first being TSS (Training Stress Score), in a widget you can see on the watch and the app.

It’ll show a bit of a breakdown of your sports:

Next, there’s CTL (Chronic Training Load), showing how this compares to recent history:

Within that, you’ll see your estimated VO2Max, as well as estimated 5K/10K/etc times. These all seemed a bit low to me (as in, both VO2Max was estimated low, and my current 5KM time seems about 1-2 mins slower than reality).

Then there’s TSB (Training Stress Balance), and it’s recommendation for me and my recent training load:

And then finally, there’s Recovery Time, looking at how you’re recovering from recent workouts. I do find the contrast between my TSB noted above and my recovery state noted below…well…notable. In theory, I should see some correlation here.

Meanwhile, within the Recovery area is where you’ll see your HRV values:

And all of this is also visible within the Suunto App as well:

Lastly, let’s quickly chat about battery during workouts. In my experience, this is falling short of my expectations. And seemingly, short of Suunto’s claims. Or more specifically, the watch’s own ability to predict battery life. In every case where I was under 20-25% battery, and the watch claimed one thing (e.g., 5-7 hours of battery remaining), the watch would run out of battery mid-activity, well below/before its own estimates.

Here’s the actual battery claims from Suunto’s site:

Here’s a simple battery example during a ride:

Start: 86%
End: 70%
Duration: 3 hours
Estimate: 5.45%/hour or 18.35hrs capacity
No navigation or external sensors enabled, multiband configuration AOD.

In this configuration, it got the 18 hours it’s rated for, but equally, every single time the estimates on the watch itself would be incorrect for what it actually burned. Meaning, I quickly came to not trust those estimates. If it said 5 hours remaining, you had at best 2-3 hours remaining.

But at least it did hit the estimates on their site. They just need to tweak whatever logic they’re using in the watch to correctly figure out battery burn.

Accuracy (GPS & Heart Rate):

In this section I’ll look at the accuracy of the new optical heart rate sensor, the upgraded GPS/GNSS chipset, as well as an occasional glance at the elevation profile, especially for mountain runs. These are compared to both a chest strap and other watch/band optical HR sensors.

First up we’ve got this mostly steady-state run, including an initial downhill portion for a few kilometers. Zero issues here, it looks good:

Next, we’ve got an interval run. This one got off to a rough start for whatever reason. But after that warm-up, things simmered down and it nailed all the intervals without issue.

Next, a trail run up/down a mountain. This had some variability in it, running with others (meaning, sometimes a bit lower HR’s). Still, overall this is pretty good. At some walking intensities, it was slightly mixed, but when actually running, it was mostly good enough.

Next, an indoor trainer ride. Here we can see it’s a bit wobbly in the first few minutes, but it gets the general trend right. After that it’s perfectly fine.

Whereas heading outside, looking at one of (many) outdoor rides, this one with lots of up and downs into the mountains, things are…shall we say, rough. Sure, it’s right for a good chunk at a time, but it’s wrong an awful lot – especially when I’m descending or at slightly lower intensities.

Switching over to the GPS side of things, starting off with a relatively straightforward run. Some occasional buildings and such, but nothing too complicated to begin:

Still, when I zoomed in, the Suunto was consistently the ‘odd duck,’ being just slightly offset from the others, even in basically open sky conditions:

Or here, where both COROS and Suunto are off in the road, playing in traffic. The Fenix 9 Pro has me properly on the sidewalk:

Next, a trail run into the mountains. Pretty straightforward up and down, but with lots of switchbacks:

Most of the trails were pretty good. Occasionally, a few quirks from different units being off a couple of meters, but nothing I was super concerned about.

Looking at the elevation profile, some slight disagreement there on the offset, but they all largely trended together. I don’t know the precise elevation of the ‘summit’ here since it’s sorta a forest service style road that just meanders along the mountains. Note: this was at/through sunset (over the course of two hours), so temps were shifting.

Next, looking at an outdoor road ride up into the mountains, from a GPS standpoint, things look perfectly fine at a high level:

And when I zoom in during some of the climbs, things are good here too:

That said, as I descend for some of these switchbacks at higher speeds, it’s a bit more Mario Kart than I’d like. I don’t tend to see this amount of variability here (into the bushes, wrong side of road, etc.), as I am from the Suunto Run 2.

Meanwhile, the elevation profile here is all good. No problems at all:

Finally, I’ve got GPS tracks from an openwater swim. Suffice to say, this was going well…till it wasn’t. No idea why it decided to slam through the side of a mountain when I didn’t. But maybe it just wanted some pool time instead. As for the swim buoy track, well…the watch fell into the water (flipped over on the strap). But you can pretty clearly see when it was above water and when it was under. Either way, the Suunto Run 2 was a hot mess here. MARQ was spot on.

Overall, I’d say that the GPS is probably perfectly acceptable for most land-based activities, but if you’re a bit nitpicky, you might not love some of the imperfections that I didn’t see on the higher-end Suunto Race 3S, or other competitive watches.

Meanwhile, for heart rate, this is a massive step up from the Suunto Run 1. While this sensor appears to struggle with outdoor cycling, for all other scenarios it’s been perfectly fine.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Wrap-Up:

The Suunto Run 2 brings with it a lot of improvements that make it a compelling upgrade over the original Suunto Run 1. While that original watch was aimed at the budget end of the spectrum, with the jump to $349, Suunto is focusing a bit more on the premium end of that budget running watch realm. For those that want a much better display, offline maps, and a better optical heart rate sensor, it’ll probably be worth that $100 jump in price.

Where Suunto gets themselves into a little bit of a pickle is they’re essentially giving up the budget end of the spectrum to COROS (with the Pace 4 and Pace Pro) and Amazfit (and even Garmin with the Forerunner 70/Vivoactive 6, sans-maps). While I think Suunto can largely justify the $349 price point with premium materials/looks, I worry that, long term, not having any current-gen Suunto watch model below this price point takes Suunto out of the running for a portion of the population. Time will tell, though; I feel like time and history already told us how this ends about 4-5 years ago, the last time Suunto tried this pricing shift and had to retreat. Adding to the complication is that the Suunto Run 2 doesn’t run the same operating system as the rest of Suunto’s watches, making it less likely to get as many new feature updates (again, as history clearly told us with the Run 1).

Nonetheless, if you view the Suunto Run 2 through the lens of what it has today, especially around the looks/materials, it’s a good option that gets the job done. Said differently, if what you see in this review, feature-wise, makes you happy…go forth!

With that, thanks for reading!
